text_fidelity_a:
Creativity for Kids Designed by You Fashion Studio, Fashion Design Kit For Kids This is an OK kit at best. Pretty much everything in the incredibly huge box could have been packed better and could have been made significantly better as well. Materials are cheap, tools are below the grade of what you'd find at the dollar store. Outfits you create for dolls with your little one will be a little awkward to put on because of the strange shapes of the decorations you're provided, and the skirts will be a little scandalous.

The saving grace of this kit is the doll model. It is effectively designed to be a Barbie doll sized, and if you're willing to take some old rags and wrecked clothes, you can use it to make some actually decent clothing articles. You can do better than this kit.
text_fidelity_b: Creativity for Kids Designed by You Fashion Studio, Fashion Design Kit For Kids

text_fidelity_a:
LEGO Star Wars Millennium Falcon 75257 Building Set - Starship Model with Finn, Chewbacca, Lando Calrissian, Boolio, C-3PO, R2-D2, and D-O Minifigures, The Rise of Skywalker Movie Collection It's a LEGO Millenium Falcon, but it's not that $800, 7000ish piece Millenium Falcon that you're thinking of from yesteryear. This is a substantially smaller version, and it's fairly easy to build with only 1,700ish pieces.

It took Daddy about 6 hours, with occasional assistance from the little one, who found this set to be "too grey" and a little overwhelming. It's true to form, and she's not a Star Wars fan, so it makes perfect sense. This set is very broad and wide, and for most of the build, you're going to be looking at adding small pieces all over the fully assembled base. Not difficult per se, but it does require a substantial attention span, and the 12+ age range seems appropriate (my daughter, LEGO expert, who can build many 400-piece sets on her own, is only 6).

The final product has an opening ceiling, a moving ramp, a smuggler's hold, a moving turret, a game area, a pilot's seat, and a kitchen. Go figure that in my set, C3PO and R2 spend a lot of time having tea parties and playing checkers. Overall, it looks great, and has a high toy value. The outer hatch is quite awkward, and doesn't connect well to the body of the main ship, and the hatch on the top connects awkwardly on the section over this same area. Other than this minor issue, the set is very cool, comes with some unique minifigs that are very different from your standard LEGO guys, and is fun even for the grey-hating, non-Star-Wars fan in my daughter.

Great.
text_fidelity_b: LEGO Star Wars Millennium Falcon 75257 Building Set - Starship Model with Finn, Chewbacca, Lando Calrissian, Boolio, C-3PO, R2-D2, and D-O Minifigures, The Rise of Skywalker Movie Collection

text_fidelity_a:
Mega Construx Halo Kinsano Cyclops Raid This Halo Tank set is a very cool set for any fan of the games. It has a few small figures that look significantly more realistic than a LEGO dude, and he even has a little rocket launcher thing that he can hold. He's a little big to fit inside the vehicle, but you can just leave him attached to the top of the tank, and it looks just as good.

The Tank itself is very interesting. I haven't built all 20 combinations, but they appear to be a combination of different kinds of turrets and treads that, combined with one another, create all of the varieties. You'll use a substantial amount of the pieces to make each construction, so you'll never have enough to truly mix and match, but there are some parts of the assembly that carry over from adaptation to adaptation. Switching these out is easy enough, but it's certainly not plug-and-play.

Overall, a fun kit that will provide plenty of customization.
text_fidelity_b: Mega Construx Halo Kinsano Cyclops Raid

text_fidelity_a: LEGO NINJAGO Lloyd’s Journey 70671 Building Kit (81 Pieces) This is a very small 81 piece LEGO set that gives you a few very small playthings and a couple of minifigs.  They'll take you a few minutes to put together each, and the kids can have a little fun, but this kit is so small, and the pieces have so little functionality, that the kit itself will not be too fun for too long.  Spend a little more and get something more worth your while.
text_fidelity_b: LEGO NINJAGO Lloyd’s Journey 70671 Building Kit (81 Pieces)

text_fidelity_a:
LEGO Star Wars: A New Hope 75244 Tantive IV Building Kit (1768 Pieces) So, I'll admit it. I stayed up most of the night to finish this one. And it's glorious!

This is an adult's plaything. I know, it says 12+ on the box, but that's probably a little young. Make no mistake about that - the manual for this one is longer than most novels that my older one is able to read on her own, and although it is a LEGO product, and her attention span is great for those, this one will challenge anyone, of any age. It's easy to see why - the vast majority of pieces for this one are white, red and grey - and because it's difficult to differentiate between the bits, it can be a bear to put together for the little ones.

Once it's together, this is a masterpiece. The figurines are cool, the detachable roofs of the spaceship allow you to see in and role play the action, and the ship is HUGE. I've put together a lot of LEGO kits lately, and this dwarfs them all.
text_fidelity_b: LEGO Star Wars: A New Hope 75244 Tantive IV Building Kit (1768 Pieces)

text_fidelity_a:
LEGO NINJAGO Lloyd's Titan Mech 70676 Ninja Toy Building Kit with Ninja Minifigures for Creative Play, Fun Action Toy Includes NINJAGO Characters Including Lloyd, Zane FS and More (876 Pieces) This is a large and intricate LEGO set that has an awful lot of little built in toys for the kids to play with. The steering functionality is particularly impressive, but it also has every other LEGO trick in the book - mini-vehicles, detachable bits, springloaded piece-sheeter, and the Ninjago spinners are all here.

As you'd expect from a large set, this one has a lot of parts, and as you'd expect from the number of features, this requires an older child with an attention span to match. There are more than a few unique pieces, and enough of them that when you eventually scrap your model for parts, you get a significant chunk that can be re-used to make another crazy vehice. The sails, and the bottom axles are both very intriguing from a usage point of view. This is one of the more difficult sets we've put together, but in the end, it's worth the effort.
text_fidelity_b: LEGO NINJAGO Lloyd's Titan Mech 70676 Ninja Toy Building Kit with Ninja Minifigures for Creative Play, Fun Action Toy Includes NINJAGO Characters Including Lloyd, Zane FS and More (876 Pieces)

text_fidelity_a:
LEGO Creator 3in1 Twin Rotor Helicopter 31096 Building Kit (569 Pieces) One of these things is not like the others. The boat is pretty standard, as is the airplane. The Helicopter is all kinds of cool. The twin rotor blades spin, the hatch in back opens, and the winch is capable of lifting the buoy that comes with the kit.

It's an interesting way to put together a 3 in one kit. We built the helicopter first. It's the most difficult build in the box, uses the most pieces, has the most complexity, and is far and away the nicest looking model. Then we took that apart to build the rather uninspiring "super fast plane" and the "awesome hovercraft" that looks just like a chubby boat. You do not have the pieces in here to build all three at once and play with them together.

It's certainly nice to have a very cool model like this, and I love that there are kits nowadays that utilize the multiple instructions. I wish that the other models were a little more in line with the helicopter.
text_fidelity_b: LEGO Creator 3in1 Twin Rotor Helicopter 31096 Building Kit (569 Pieces)

text_fidelity_a:
LEGO City Fire Chief Response Truck 60231 Building Kit (201 Pieces) This simple fire truck set is an easy build that looks OK on the table. My daughter likes the model, but she's 5 and has a low standard when it comes to LEGO. For her, if it's made with blocks, it looks excellent and is fun. I think it looks like a pickup truck that was painted red. The water cannon does not attach nicely to the truck piece itself, although you can manipulate it to make it work, and it has the same little launcher mechanism that most LEGO kits incorporate nowadays.

Overall, this one isn't the best kit, in my opinion - LEGO has made far better looking and more challenging fire truck models even - but this will work, and it's LEGO, so it's going to be fun for kids to add to the collection regardless.

text_fidelity_a:
LEGO Hidden Side Graveyard Mystery 70420 Building Kit, App Toy for 7+ Year Old Boys and Girls, Interactive Augmented Reality Playset (335 Pieces) I hope they don't overdo it, but this new LEGO Augmented Reality system is quite cool.

There is an app that you download to your phone, and using that app, you can view your LEGO set, and watch it move and change a little bit. If you've seen someone playing Pokemon Go or using a filter on their camera phone, you'll get the idea. It works surprisingly well given that it's easy to slightly alter the design. The app itself is downloadable on iTunes and Android, and works well on the Android system, although you really likely want to use a phone because of the size of the tablet. It will work, but it gets in the way of play.

Like all parents, I'm not entirely thrilled about yet another excuse to hand over my phone, but I think that the augmented reality piece is really more of a gimmick that my daughter will tire of sooner rather than later. The building of the set must come first in order for this to work, and that's mildly educational, and we get to play with the LEGO set without the phone as well.

And did I mention how cool this set is, even without the augmented reality? The ghost theme makes for some cool pieces, and I like how this one looks when it's done. It's a winner.
text_fidelity_b: LEGO Hidden Side Graveyard Mystery 70420 Building Kit, App Toy for 7+ Year Old Boys and Girls, Interactive Augmented Reality Playset (335 Pieces)

text_fidelity_a:
LEGO Friends Olivia’s Summer Heart Box 41387 Building Kit (93 Pieces) (Discontinued by Manufacturer) I love LEGO kits, especially the small ones. It's amazing what you can do with 30 white blocks and five odd-shaped orange ones in the pelican kit, or how you can take a few small bits and turn them into an archway or a doorway. text_fidelity_a:
The Chameleon, Award-Winning Board Game for Families & Friends…… If you're familiar with the game Spyfall, then you're going to be able to jump right into this game. This one is quirkier, faster, but fortunately, has more replayability than Spyfall does.

In The Chameleon, each player is given a code card, or a card that says "You're the Chameleon." If you have a code card, you look up a word on a shared board, and if you're The Chameleon, you attempt to blend in with everyone else. After a little bit of finding and thinking time, each player says one word, even the Chameleon. Each player is then to attempt to argue and deduce who the Chameleon player is. Everyone votes, and that player is revealed. If it's not the Chameleon, then that player has done a good job of blending in and is the winner of the round. If it is the Chameleon, then that player gets the opportunity to guess the secret word that everyone else knew. If they get it right, they win. If not, everyone else wins.

Rounds of this game are fast, and that's a great thing. After repeat plays, it becomes fairly easy to identify the Chameleon player, but that's when the game really starts. Were you vague enough with your words so that they cannot figure out the secret code word?

There is enough replayability in this box to make the game fun for a wide range of groups, and a larger number of players. There are 40 different category clues, which means that there are 640 different possible words you could have, and that far exceeds the 20 locations of Spyfall.

Two issues prevent this from being a 5* game. The first is component quality. It's bad. Cards are awkwardly sized and flimsy, there are remainder marks on the edges of some cards from where they were cut. The second issue is that there simply aren't enough mapping location cards in the box. There's really only two possible sets of locations, and while there are no players who will be able to memorize the exact locations of words, it's possible that repeat mappings occur, and Chameleons with outstanding memories will be able to guess with regularity by reading the dice.
text_fidelity_b: The Chameleon, Award-Winning Board Game for Families & Friends……

text_fidelity_a:
Sew Mini Gardens (Klutz Craft Kit) The Klutz kits are hit and miss for us, but this one was a hit. Now, that said, like a lot of the Klutz kits, this is a difficult one for children, and will require a very hands on adult helper.

The designs are very nice, and the instructions are good throughout if you have Google or sewing knowledge. It's not that it's going to be terribly difficult to figure out how to sew necessarily, but some of the designs are reasonably complex. I'm not a sewer, but I could figure it out, and instruct my little ones. There are a lot of steps to some of them, and the dexterity needed means that this is going to be one for the older children almost exclusively - they'll need some "advanced" skills like maintaining an even stitch pattern that is not too widely spaced or narrow, figuring out what "whip-stitching" is without it being explained thoroughly, and so forth. Because the designs are all fairly small, you can make one, then save the rest for later, and the kit will see use for many crafting sessions.

I'm very impressed by the finished product as well. Overall, a fun and educational experience for the little ones and for myself as well.
text_fidelity_b: Sew Mini Gardens (Klutz Craft Kit)

text_fidelity_a:
Escape Room in a Box: Flashback, Escape Room Game with 19 Puzzles and 4 Locks, Can Pair with Amazon Alexa, For Adults and Teens 13 Years Old and Up It's an 80s themed box, with a name like "Flashback" that has nothing to do with the 80s, and very little to do with "flashbacks". It's actually about werewolves, a magic ring, and bad poetry. The story makes no sense at all, and that's the easiest element of an escape room, really. Fortunately, everything else in this box is pretty good.

We played with a group of 4 people, which was perfect. You could even do six and have a great time with it. The game is broken into three paths - red, purple and blue, each with a very vague theme like "poems" (blue), "childhood" (purple) and "dinosaurs" (red) - and you need to complete all three in order to win. We broke our group of four into two teams of two and tackled blue and purple envelopes separately, then worked together on the red and the final puzzle. Each envelope took us roughly the same amount of time to beat, and the final puzzle was appropriately paced to be solved quickly. Most other escape room games we've played, from Unlock to Exit to Escape the Room all suffer from pacing problems, or narrowing you down to having only one puzzle or a few cards to work with at one time, which is nice for pointing out the way to solve some more complex puzzles, but which makes it rather difficult to play with more than two people - this box has solved that problem.

Overall, we were pretty impressed with this with a few caveats. One of the puzzles requires you to do something to the game pieces that is spelled out early on in the letter. It wasn't difficult to figure out what to do, but it was difficult to execute. It's hard to say more without giving out spoilers for one of the "coolest" puzzles in the box, but let's just say that it was mechanically difficult to work with. One of the puzzles at the end of the game required another outside prop that's easy to deal with, but the amount of finagleing with the pieces and the prop left us questioning if we had solved that puzzle correctly (we did, but it wasn't quite clear).

One touch that I particularly liked was how the game color-coded everything according to the paths/envelopes, and how the locked boxes worked - they performed exacly as they should have, and they were high enough quality that we felt like we could toss them around a little without any issues.

This is expensive for a one-time-use product, but it's definitely my favorite of the escape room games for a medium to large sized group, and it's probably pretty good for two slueths to solve on their own as well.

Solved in 1:07:11.
text_fidelity_b: Escape Room in a Box: Flashback, Escape Room Game with 19 Puzzles and 4 Locks, Can Pair with Amazon Alexa, For Adults and Teens 13 Years Old and Up

text_fidelity_a:
Made By Me 3-in-1 Lots of Knots Fleece Activity Kit by Horizon Group USA, Pre-Cut Fabric Squares, No Sewing, No Cutting, Felt Decals, Make a Fleece Quilt, Fringe Purse & Jumbo Pillow This is a great idea, especially as my daughter has always struggled with tying. She was one of the last in her age range to tie her shoes on her own, so I was hoping that this kit would encourage her to work with it a little more. She struggled, which I fully expected. Then Daddy struggled. Then Mama struggled. Then I realized that this kit is just difficult.

Everything in here is precut and premade. There's only one step - putting things together and tying. And that's where the problem comes in. The ties are too short or too thick. They won't stay together well once they're tied on, and some pieces are poorly sized compared to others.

I will admit that we did complete one of the projects, and it looks pretty good. It was a lot of effort, and felt very lucky when compared to the rest of the kit, but it did work.

I wish this was better, but it's knot (had to put a Dad joke in there!).
text_fidelity_b: Made By Me 3-in-1 Lots of Knots Fleece Activity Kit by Horizon Group USA, Pre-Cut Fabric Squares, No Sewing, No Cutting, Felt Decals, Make a Fleece Quilt, Fringe Purse & Jumbo Pillow

text_fidelity_a:
ALEX Toys Scientific Explorer Bee-Ology Science Kids Science Experiment Kit This is an interesting kit, that in all fairness should probably be about a 3.5 star product, but Amazon forces me to choose, so I'll rank this on the lower end.

There is a lot to like here - the activities are pretty good, the variety is great, and the educational value is fantastic. My daughter's favorite were the bee goggles, which was the simplest activity, while I liked the idea of building the model to identify the parts of the bee. There are some simple chits that you can move around to organize a hive that look like they belong in a board game, but didn't provide a lot of interest for daughter.

There are plenty of opportunities as well. The book that comes with the set is a big miss. There is a ton of information inside that helped me answer some questions for my daughter, but it is dry as a bone, and holds no interest for her whatsoever. It's essentially an encyclopedia entry about bees, and educationally, it's fabulous, but from a kid's point of view, they forgot to include anything fun.

There is one activity that requires you have a live flower, so that will be a miss for anyone doing this kit over a fall or winter season unless they want to take a separate trip to the store.

As I said above, there were 5 activities, and while I liked one or two, there's not too much to some of them. Pollinate a flower? OK, that's done in a few minutes. Bee wings buzzing? A fun toy, not too much really make use of here. The goggles were a hit with the kid, but are a dress up accessory at best for me. The model was great. The peel and stick bit was a good idea that didn't resonate with my little one.

Overall, it's a good idea, especially given the season we've tried it in, and in combination with our outdoor bee sanctuaries and veggie garden. Giving kids an education about these pollinators is important and could be a fantastic idea for the future, but for this kit, I think there's room for improvement.
text_fidelity_b: ALEX Toys Scientific Explorer Bee-Ology Science Kids Science Experiment Kit

text_fidelity_a:
Mega Pokemon Froakie vs. Dedenne Construx Set A nice littel kit for kids that is an ideal "first" MegaConstrux box to play with. Mega Construx are compatible with LEGO kits, but they tend to be a little harder to build, contain more flat pieces, look a lot better, and have much harder to decpher instructions. This one had no issues with the instructions, and was very simple to make thanks to the low number of pieces.

That said, it is built very quickly, and the level of detail on these figures is lower that your traditional Mega Construx set. Pikachu and Chimchar are smaller than average figures, but there are some cool scenery bits that can be played with as well.

A kid could have a great time with this.

Mega Pokemon Construx 188 Piece Building Set | Slashing Scyther This Pokemon set is the best Mega Construx build I've ever done.

Like all Mega Construx items it will have lots of flat pieces, mediocre instructions that will be difficult for younger kids, and it will look absolutely fantastic when you compare it to a similarly priced LEGO set. This kit is great though. It has a twisting motion built in, so it ends up working a bit like an action figure, and the tree falls apart when the Scyther strikes it. It is difficult to recommend to younger kids because it is a bit difficult to build and has lots of smaller pieces. For an avid LEGO lover who's had some practice or any adult, this is a great kit.

text_fidelity_a:
Winning Moves Games Pretty Princess Board Game I am a board game afficionado. I own over 200 different strategy, social or silly games, and you'd better believe that my daughter is a gamer in waiting. Of course, as a young boy, Pretty Pretty Princess wasn't on my radar for myself, but I knew the name and the concept, and when it was my time to find a copy for my kid, there's no way I was paying the multiple hundreds for the original 80's item.

So I was thrilled when an appropriately priced remake made it's way to my house, and all it took was reading the name to hook my daughter (and interestingly, my wife as well) into a quest to become the most beautiful in all the realm.

The box for this one opens upside down for some reason, and one you get inside, you'll find a spinner, an odd, nearly blank game board, and some teeny tiny jewels to bling out your ensemble. Play is simple - you spin the spinner, attempt to move aroudn the circular board to earn all your gems, and the first one to get everything is crowned (literally) the prettiest princess.

Perhaps the most striking thing is the lack of effort they put into the board and spinner. Both are of reasonable thickness and sturdy, but there is almost nothing on the board in terms of graphic design outside of the logo on the field of white, and the spinner is literally numbers. They may have changed the font away from Times New Roman, but that's all there is to it. It looks like a high school kid's graphic design project, and not one that's going to earn high marks from the teacher.

That said, it's good to have this game back in print again, even if the game play is not particularly solid, and even if the graphics leave quite a bit to be desired. As I said, all I needed to do to get my little one to play was to tell her the name of the game, and my wife jumped right in on the nostalgia boat as well.
text_fidelity_b: Winning Moves Games Pretty Princess Board Game

text_fidelity_a:
Mega Construx Pokemon Detective Pikachu Hi-hat Café Construction Set with character figures, Building Toys for Kids (328 Pieces) Mega Construx blocks are compatible with LEGO brand blocks, but they have a different focus. In general, they focus on looking nicer, having smaller pieces with smooth edges, and are much more difficult to turn into an off-script creation. Also, they tend to have terrible instruction books, and this kit is no different.

The assembly requires a bit of imagination and guessing, and the kit is not packaged particularly well, as it often requires opening many bags at once to remove the singular small pieces referenced in the manual. Because of this, the kit is harder to assemble than your average LEGO set, but I have to admit that it looks pretty cool when it's done. There are not nearly as many LEGO pegs sticking out as you get on a typical LEGO build, and the figures articulate quite a bit more naturally.

Overall a fun kit for slightly more patient and experienced builders.
text_fidelity_b: Mega Construx Pokemon Detective Pikachu Hi-hat Café Construction Set with character figures, Building Toys for Kids (328 Pieces)

text_fidelity_a:
Klutz Mini Eraser Animals Craft Kit Brown/a This is a very small craft kit that comes with enough modeling clay to make fifteen erasers, according to the box at least. We ended up with 12, which is close enough. There is a book that includes instructions for how to create a few basic shapes, or you can just free form create whatever creatures you want, and there is a shaping tool made out of a cheap piece of plastic - a few toothpicks work just as well. The biggest problem is that these are "erasers" and well...they don't really erase particularly well. So they're really mostly just bite-sized statues.

LEGO The Movie 2 Queen Watevra’s ‘So-Not-Evil’ Space Palace 70838 Building Kit (995 Pieces) (Discontinued by Manufacturer) I think that the things you get from the Lego Movie 2 kits have a tendency to look a mess, but my daughter loves it, so who am I to complain. text_fidelity_a:
Arcade Claw Game: Maker Lab (Klutz STEM Kit) Brown/a, 9.8" x 2.5" x 11.8" The promise of this kit is that it's difficult. The final product, if it works according to specifications, looks amazing, and should teach some important concepts in a fun and interesting way. And this kit does accomplish a lot of what it sets out to do - it's hard to build, requires a little dexterity, and does work reasonably well after construction is complete - all while being a fun teaching tool.

This kit is labeled for use with smaller kids, but realistically a child will need to be around age nine or so to build this with minimal assistance from an adult. There are many steps, and it requires the ability to tie knots, balance pieces, and do some basic measurement.

Perhaps the strongest element of this kit is the booklet - steps are clear and easy to follow, although there are quite a few of them before a finished product is complete - and it does have a brief introduction that teaches the concepts of pulleys.

The downside of this kit is that, yes, it's difficult and time consuming. Unless your kid is an engineer in the making, it will require parental assistance. It's easy to quit, and if you do decide to leave it in the middle, it can be difficult to pick up where you left off. That said, difficulty is something that a lot of us want, so if you know it going in, then it's no big deal. The final product promises a lot, and surprisingly, it delivers, but the plastic side panels that hold the kit together are a bit flimsy, and require extra support.

Overall, we're impressed.
text_fidelity_b: Arcade Claw Game: Maker Lab (Klutz STEM Kit) Brown/a, 9.8" x 2.5" x 11.8"

text_fidelity_a: LEGO City Dock Side Fire 60213 Building Kit (97 Pieces) This will take a half-hour or less to put together.  It's a very simple design and has enough play value to make this a good kit to buy, but the value for building time might not be there.  In reality, this is not that much larger than many of the bagged kits. If you don't mind paying a little bit more for a Lego kit, this is a fun one,and there really aren't that many boats out there.
text_fidelity_b: LEGO City Dock Side Fire 60213 Building Kit (97 Pieces)

text_fidelity_a: LEGO NINJAGO Legacy Golden Dragon 70666 Building Kit (171 Pieces) This kit is a looker, not a player.  The fins that stick off of the Dragon are very easy to break off and delicate.  It's not specifically difficult to put back together, but with the modern deisgns of Lego being very action and fighting oriented, this one will not stand up to a beating.  If you want to put it on a shelf, this kit will work great, and it's easy to put together with really simple instructions.
text_fidelity_b: LEGO NINJAGO Legacy Golden Dragon 70666 Building Kit (171 Pieces)

text_fidelity_a:
LEGO Friends Olivia's Cupcake Café 41366 Building Kit (335 Pieces) This is a great playsetfor any young girl. It's not very difficult to put togeher at all, and it comes with a wide variety of unique pieces, from the mixer to the whisk and signage. There's enough room once it's together for the figures to move around and interact inside the shop, and enough little mini-areas around the kit for there to be plenty for them to do.

A good beginner's set for anyone of about 5 and up.
text_fidelity_b: LEGO Friends Olivia's Cupcake Café 41366 Building Kit (335 Pieces)

text_fidelity_a:
Craft-tastic – Jewelry Branch Kit – Craft Kit Makes One 16” Jewelry Holder With this kit, your child will make a rather flimsy little cardboard branch that is ostensibly meant to hold jewelry. The instructions are well-written, and the project is not terribly difficult to do. Your kids will likely not need much help from Mom and Dad outside of a little quality control - this one's a little easy to mess up if you aren't winding it tightly.

I think the final product is pretty weak. It's clearly made of cardboard, and that's evident from the moment you attempt to touch or use it. It's an awkward thing to mount or use, and even my girls don't really want to use it. Fun to make for an hour or two though.
text_fidelity_b: Craft-tastic – Jewelry Branch Kit – Craft Kit Makes One 16” Jewelry Holder

text_fidelity_a:
Ludonaute Fantasy Flight Games LUCV01 Carta Imperia Victoria, Multicolor CIV is a very good small card game. It takes about a half hour to play, and is largely comprised of cards with silly cartoonish art on them representing science, military, culture and so forth. Basically, if it's in Sid Meier's Civilization, it has been boiled down and reduced to a small concept here.

The artwork is...interesting. Some people will love it's uniqueness, while others will find it to be off-putting. I tend to fall in the latter column - it doesn't look like it matches with the theme of the game at all. The player aids are good, but small (probably to fit in the box), and can be difficult to read. It would have been better, in my opinion, to put some more text on each individual card instead of trying to stuff all the text onto one very small aid.

These are quibbles. The game is fast, interesting, and offers some good decision-making along the way.
text_fidelity_b: Ludonaute Fantasy Flight Games LUCV01 Carta Imperia Victoria, Multicolor

text_fidelity_a:
LEGO The Movie 2 Pop-Up Party Bus 70828 Building Kit, Build Your Own Toy Party Bus for 9+ Year Old Girls and Boys (1013 Pieces) (Discontinued by Manufacturer) I like this set much more than my daughter does. This set is over 1,000 pieces, making it a very difficult build for younger players, but it does have a lot of individual elements that make up this particular set. There are multiple levels within the vehicle, elements that unfold or open up, and each is constructed separately. Ultimately, you'll feel good about the fact that you've done it, but both of us have to admit that the end result is less impressive than some of the other sets that we've built together recently. This is compact, and not outwardly "cool" as it's really just an awkwardly shaped bus that could double as a spaceship. The characters are in line with the "Friends" series, so they definitely look like they don't belong with many of the basic sets. There is some play value here, but once you play with the folding and unfolding, there's less here than it appears.

Overall, if you're a fan of the movies, this may be an essential item. For us, it was a challenging pass.
text_fidelity_b: LEGO The Movie 2 Pop-Up Party Bus 70828 Building Kit, Build Your Own Toy Party Bus for 9+ Year Old Girls and Boys (1013 Pieces) (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

text_fidelity_a:
LEGO Overwatch D.Va and Reinhardt 75973 Mech Building Kit with Popular Overwatch Character Minifigures and Buildable Rocket Hammer (455 Pieces) Neither my daughter nor I play Overwatch, but we do enjoy our Lego products together. I got this expecting to get some cool robots that would likely be invited over to tea with Barbie, but what I did not expect was how great these would look assembled. These robots have intricate touches on their armor that look really unique, and often hide the tell-tale Lego look that many of their creations have. The result is that these look more like real toys than something we put together.

There are a few minor quibbles. This comes with a lot of rare or unique pieces, but unlike a lot of kits, I have difficulty imagining using many of them beyond the specific applications of putting these kits together. A lot of very intricate and small pieces make these work. In addition, one of the figures slots into their robot perfectly, while the other is just tossed into a slot to rattle around, which feels pretty unfinished. A decidedly non-professional touch to a kit that would otherwise be worthy of display.

Overall though, a great character kit from Lego.
text_fidelity_b: LEGO Overwatch D.Va and Reinhardt 75973 Mech Building Kit with Popular Overwatch Character Minifigures and Buildable Rocket Hammer (455 Pieces)

text_fidelity_a:
WILD! Science Cake of Soap Factory - Science Kits for Kids - STEM - Make Your Own Soap Experiments This is a fun STEM kit that's on the simple side - our 5-year-old needed help, but not much. Anyone of reading age should be able to complete the whole thing entirely on their own. This kit makes little soaps that look like baked goods - cookies, cupcakes, macaroons, etc.

The project itself is relatively short - it took us about two hours working slowly - but the finished products look great, and have a purpose. Kids will learn many kitchen skills as well - stirring to look for consistency in the mixture, the vision and patience to look for setting molds, loading and using a piping bag.

All told, one of the best kits we've finished.
text_fidelity_b: WILD! Science Cake of Soap Factory - Science Kits for Kids - STEM - Make Your Own Soap Experiments

text_fidelity_a:
LEGO Super Heroes Marvel Spider Mech Vs. Venom 76115 Action Toy Building Kit with Web Shooter and Gripping Toy Claw Includes Spider-Man Minifigures Venom and Ghost Spider (604 Pieces) This is a cooler-than-average lego set for a more advanced builder. There are a number of more unique pieces included in this setup, and while I don't know quite what you'd use many of them for outside of building this specific kit, I'm sure your kids would. The kit, as assembled, is slightly more difficult than most because a lot of the details are small and there are a surpising number of pieces in the robot and monster respectively. This helps them stand up to a lot more punsihment without falling apart.

A great lego product, especially if you want ones to play with as opposed to having a strict building setup.
text_fidelity_b: LEGO Super Heroes Marvel Spider Mech Vs. Venom 76115 Action Toy Building Kit with Web Shooter and Gripping Toy Claw Includes Spider-Man Minifigures Venom and Ghost Spider (604 Pieces)

text_fidelity_a:
Bezier Games One Week Ultimate Werewolf "Werewolf" games from Bezier games are becoming a bit ubiquitous at this point. That said, the core gameplay of the original, and certain spinoff titles like Inquisition have worked well for me in the past. "One Night" never really floated my boat, as it was too short and chaotic, so the "One Week" version seemed like a good fit.

In this game, you're moving around a castle board searching for Werewolves. You can do many "One Night" things - switch tokens without knowing who you are or who you become, and you need to bluff about which cards you are using. Unfortunately, this game shares a little too much from many of the same flaws that I noticed with One Night Ultimate Werewolf - it's too chaotic, it's still too quick, and you still will struggle to make strategic decisions because you don't often know what you are doing when you take actions. For people who enjoy the strategy-less designer games, like Talisman or traditional Werewolf, then this might be a hit if you have the right group.

For the right group, this will be a big success. While I do like it more than "One Night", it's not quite ready for my tastes yet.
text_fidelity_b: Bezier Games One Week Ultimate Werewolf

text_fidelity_a:
Klutz Grow Your Own Crystal Mini Worlds Craft and Science Kit The "Grow your own Crystal Mini Worlds" kit is a good one. It is a bit complicated compared to other craft kits of it's ilk, and requires a good amount of time, planning, and careful activation and storage of the key components, as you'll use things from project to project.

The crafts themselves are pretty impressive as well. The crystals all grew for me, which is often something that we struggle with in our home with other crystal growing kits, and the number of differnt ways your children can put them together is quite impressive. There is some modeling clay that can help with creating unique items, and there are a number of different design elements as well.

The biggest drawbacks are twofold - this requires older children, and it will definitely require more adult supervision and planning than your average arts and crafts kit, not only in terms of handling the heating, but also in aiding in the planning and reading stages of craft creation. Additionally, while I've become used to having crafting materials stored all around my home, this one takes the cake in terms of storing solutions, setting up crystal growing areas that cannot be disturbed, drying areas, and set up areas that will take over your crafting area (or in my case, the dining room) for multiple nights to multiple weeks if you make your way through projects quickly.
text_fidelity_b: Klutz Grow Your Own Crystal Mini Worlds Craft and Science Kit

text_fidelity_a:
Repos JUST01 Just One, Various There are a lot of "just one word clues" games out there, from Codenames and Decrypto to games like Funglish, Crosstalk or Word Slam, and this game is yet another to add to that group. I think, however, that it's my secnd favorite of the bunch, and if you need a Codenames Killer, this might be up your alley.

In this team game, one player is attempting to guess a word that the rest of their team knows. Each team member writes down one word only, then compares to see if any matches are detected. If they are, those cards are discarded, and the guesser is left with fewer clues. Therefore, the more obtuse clues you get, the more you'll have, but it can be more difficult to deduce the word than if you're given a few obvious clues.

What I like about this game is that it manages to be a louder than usual team game with secrets. In Codenames or Crosstalk, two previous iterations of the concept, games are fun, but often it's players staring at the board in silence. In this one, you still can't say much, but it does lend itself to quicker play, and it's easier to communicate more freely once you have your clues written since your work is done, and the stress of the round is over for the clue-givers. This is a hard game, and it's definitely a word game, but lends itself to being an excellent family gathering game.
text_fidelity_b: Repos JUST01 Just One, Various

text_fidelity_a:
Klutz Air Blast Cannon: Maker Lab STEM Kit, Multi-Colored, 9.8"" x 2.5"" x 11.8""" The final product is pretty disappointing. The "blast" is more like a puff, and while the kit is not too hard to put together, it is difficult to operate and play with. Whie my daughter didn't seem to care about that so much, Dad felt like this should have worked a lot better considering how much it costs.

That said, when you buy a product like this, most of the fun is had putting the toy together, and for that, the instructions were well laid out and thought through, and it wasn't overly difficult. Minimal parent support was needed, although I did doube check to make sure things were good before we tried shooting rockets. They did not fly far, or fast, and they were a pain to load onto the machine.
text_fidelity_b: Klutz Air Blast Cannon: Maker Lab STEM Kit, Multi-Colored, 9.8"" x 2.5"" x 11.8"""

text_fidelity_a:
Bézier Games Ultimate Werewolf Revised Edition Werewolf is not usually a "game night" game that you play with a group of friends. I've always used it in classroom settings, or with larger groups, usually upwards of 10 people, where this game really shines. Ultimately, Werewolf is a deduction game in which most players are Villagers, unwittingly being killed or eliminated by a sect of Werewolf players. Using very limited clues and knowledge, it's up to the Villagers to unmask the Werewolves and eliminate them from the game before they themselves are eaten.

The only real issue that I have with Werewolf is that there is player elimination, although since Werewolf is not a particularly long game, it's usually OK, and bystanders often have as much fun as the players.

There are plenty of versions of this game available out there, but I think that Bezier's "Ultimate" is certainly the way to go. The bits are durable and well made, and there are enough cards to play an 80 person game. That said, there is less content in here as compared to the "Revised Edition" that came out a few years ago. I still think that this is the box to get, however, as the roles and unique playing styles presented in the "Revised" box are more complicated, and not really in line with the casual spirit of the game. I think they certainly provide more variety, but at the expense of complicating the players and making it far more difficult for the moderator. As it's impossible to answer questions mid-game, it's best to leave the complicated roles to a different genre of game.

A 5-Star Product for sure.
text_fidelity_b: Bézier Games Ultimate Werewolf Revised Edition

text_fidelity_a:
Thames & Kosmos Word Slam Family | Fast-Paced Multiplayer Party Card & Word Game | High Playercount | Based On The Award Winning Word Slam Word Slam Family is a nice game that's easy to play, despite the dense rule sheet that comes with the game. You can set this up and play it quickly, and it's easy enough that it truly is a family weight game. You don't even need to be a reader to get some of the clues, assuming an adult is there to help.

That said, this game is a very straightforward, and less interesting game than the hundreds that are just like it, but with a twist (Decrypto, Codenames, Funglish, Crosstalk, Insider, Werewords, When I Dream, etc). It's a one-word for one-word style association game, that, quite frankly, is done better by most of it's competitors. I think that this one might appeal to those who really like the small box size, or who haven't played any competitors, but as someone who has, this adds nothing new to the genre, and does not have the staying power of it's rivals.
text_fidelity_b: Thames & Kosmos Word Slam Family | Fast-Paced Multiplayer Party Card & Word Game | High Playercount | Based On The Award Winning Word Slam

text_fidelity_a: Thames & Kosmos 555063 Engineering Makerspace Off-Road Rovers Science Experiment Kit This is a simpler STEM kit that offers light-weight models you can assembe quite quickly.  My daughter has plenty of experience with STEM model building, and she was able to assemble these with minimal help.  The box clearly states that this product is for ages 6 and up, which might highlight the fact that these models are a good bit simpler than others by the same company, and rest assured that they are.  There are other kits that aim higher in age level and difficulty.  This makes an outstanding present for the younger builders out there, but older or more advanced kids might want something more robust.
text_fidelity_b: Thames & Kosmos 555063 Engineering Makerspace Off-Road Rovers Science Experiment Kit

text_fidelity_a: Thames & Kosmos Big Engineering Makerspace | Science Kit | 22 Physics Lessons & Experiments | Toy of The Year Award Finalist | Homeschool | Learning Pod | STEM Kit This is a 200+ piece kit, with the abiliy to create some 20 models out of the box.  Some are, admittedly, unspectacular - the surveyor's measuring wheel is litle more than a wheel with a stick attached, and takes less than 10 minutes to put together - but some of the more advanced models are quite intricate, and all of them have moving parts.  This is a great kit for someone who is experienced in building, because the models are better than many others I've seen, or for someone who is fairly new to the STEM kit experience, because there is something in here that anyone can build, with or without parent assistance.  This one has the widest array of models that I've seen, and all of the parts are interchangable and quite durable.  My highest recommendation

text_fidelity_a: LEGO Disney Princess 6213312 Rapunzel's Bedroom 41156 Castle This is a really great Lego Set.  Outside of all the typical benefits of having tons of new Lego pieces, this one comes with a wide variety of unique pieces that can be added to a lot of playsets.  There are some cool lanters, Pascal, and a painting of him, and many more pieces included in the set.  My daughter put it together in about 45 minutes with only a little help from Dad, and will have lots of fun with it.
text_fidelity_b: LEGO Disney Princess 6213312 Rapunzel's Bedroom 41156 Castle

text_fidelity_a:
Bezier Games Werewords Deluxe Edition I very much liked the original edition of Werewords (essentially the same game as Insider), and this is the same game, but there's more of it.

Werewords is a lot like "20 questions". Players ask yes/no questions in an attempt to identify a word that could be anything from "spatula" to "Mjollnir". One player is a werewolf, who knows the word already, and is attempting to guide the players with their questioning closer to the actual word without them figuring out that they know the word already. They win if players can identify the word, but do not know which among them is the werewolf. If they do identify the werewolf, then the werewolf can also identify the "seer" player (another with information about the word).

The deluxe edition contains a few additional roles for players. If you already have the other version of this game, I don't think you need to own this version unless you're a completionist. If you don't own any versions of this game, I think it's quite good.

My concern remains the same as before - the app for this game is good, and it doesn't appear to be going anywhere, but if you don't want to run an app while playing this game, then I totally understand, and this game will not be for you at all. I think the app does a good job of balancing the words against one another, creating the ability to discern easy from very difficult words, but the same effect could have been accomplished with cards. I would prefer the cards as well, but the app has the advantage of saving shelf space and also having a larger directory of words. In the end, it's a toss up, but if you don't mind the app, then this is the best possible edition of the game to get.
text_fidelity_b: Bezier Games Werewords Deluxe Edition

text_fidelity_a:
Thames & Kosmos Drop It | Super Fun Family Strategy Game | Parents' Choice Silver Award Winner, Multi-Color Drop It is a simple game - you drop shapes into a Plinko-like contraption,, and depending on what happens when they fall, you earn points, so long as you follow some simple placement rules - you cannot touch the same shapes or colors, and the edges have restrictions on what shapes can touch them. It's so simple, and yet it's incredibly fun.

Not only is this a fun game though, it's a game that really teaches young players how to formulate an argument, identify problems with shape placement, and think about how and what to play. I played with a five-year-old who has no strategic ability yet, but who was able to, after just one play, identify if a shape was correctly placed right away and push forward with better strategy in her second game. The older child was better able to adapt, but also showed great ability to arrange and save her shapes for times when they'd be advantageous for use.

My one concern with this game is that it is quite a bit more difficult with three players, since that is the player count in which only three of the four colors are in use, and it's harder to place pieces. This is easily remedied by a simple rules change.

This is one of the best kids games I've ever played, and far and away one of the best games I've played recently. Get it.
text_fidelity_b: Thames & Kosmos Drop It | Super Fun Family Strategy Game | Parents' Choice Silver Award Winner, Multi-Color

text_fidelity_a:
Thames & Kosmos Lost Cities: Rivals Card Game | Strategy Auction Adventure | Vibrant Colors for Two to Four Players | Family Friendly Fun by Kosmos This is the third major rendition of the "Lost Cities" games (the card game, the board game, and now Rivals). Each is a game that is ostensibly about discovering lost cities, but is really about putting numbered cards in order. None are special games in my collection, although I now own all three, and all are well-loved by some gamers in the world. Rivals is potentially the most interesting of them, as it introduces a new auction mechanic into the standard put-numbers-in-order formula, but while I found this auction to be a new and interesting method of getting cards, the two other people who I've played it with are not convinced that it's fun so much as it's mean.

I think if you don't mind a game where you play one on one and directly attack others, then this might be something you can handle. I believe that while the others are light-hearted and super easy for anyone to pick up, this suffers from the "meanness" problem, and also from the fact that the more experienced player will easily dispatch newcomers. As many who love Lost CIities have a partner in mind for when they play, and tend not to play with outsiders, this may not be a problem for Rivals, but this is certainly more intense of a "game" than those, and is not always the light hearted fare that the old classics tend to be.

If you want a light, non-interactive card game, then the other Lost Cities are better choices. If you need something more interesting, then this is a good chocie.
text_fidelity_b: Thames & Kosmos Lost Cities: Rivals Card Game | Strategy Auction Adventure | Vibrant Colors for Two to Four Players | Family Friendly Fun by Kosmos

text_fidelity_a:
ThinkFun Shadows in the Forest Play in the Dark Board Game for Kids and Families Age 8 and Up - Fun and Easy to Learn with Innovative and Unique Gameplay This is a really fun "spooky" game for kids. It's not really that "spooky", but it does require that you play in the dark, which can be a bit difficult for the very young, but fortunately the large hiding place pieces and the very cute shadowlings got our daughter to play the game willingly.

This is a hide-and-seek style of game in which one player moves a real, working lantern around the board trying to illuminate the shadowlings. It uses the old fashioned "roll and move" mechanic, but fortunately, the game does a good job of ensuring that you can usually get where you need to go. This is the role best suited to younger children.

Other children, or parents, will play as the Shadowlings. The lantern player closes their eyes, while the other players move shadowlings that are not illuminated in an attempt to hide them from the lantern-holding player. This role is better for adults because the rules are a little vague and open to interpretation in this area. Technically, you are allowed to move anywhere, so long as you are not illuminated and I think that's difficult for children to judge fairly (even the adults had an argument about it).

Overall, this is a good kids game, and adults can have some fun too. I wish the rules were a little clearer on how to lay out terrain, what "illuminated' really means, and so forth, but then again, too much of that would make the manual unreadable. Maybe some picture examples would have been ideal. As it is, your children will need some experience with this game with parents before you can let them play alone, but it is clever and, unlike many children's games, it's good for parents too.
text_fidelity_b: ThinkFun Shadows in the Forest Play in the Dark Board Game for Kids and Families Age 8 and Up - Fun and Easy to Learn with Innovative and Unique Gameplay

text_fidelity_a:
Bezier Games Werebeasts Ted Alspach and his Bezier Games companies bring us another small-box Werewolf themed game. This game shares a similar deception element, and artwork with previous releases, but like "Werewords", this is not a mainline Werewolf game or expansion.

In this game, players are auctioning off beasts of various types, and players are bidding on these creatures, whether they truly want them or not. This is because one major mechanic of the game is calling other players out on collecting specific types of creatures - if you are correct that they are hoarding a specific creature-type, then they are punished

Ultimately, this game did not appeal to us. It has a learning curve to playing, but once you get the hang of it, it makes the game feel a little too random. No matter what you really want, you need to either make a large number of offers, or make remarkable guesses about which goals other players have. Both are legitimate ways to win, but like a more standard "classic" board game, there is a definite strategy that you want to use, and there isn't a lot of replayability in this one for our group.

In our group, the only player who really liked it was the winner, and even she wasn't entirely sold on this one. It's fast, and simple, but it's a little too easy to make guesses on what other players want, and the artwork is strange.
text_fidelity_b: Bezier Games Werebeasts

text_fidelity_a:
Bezier Games Palace of Mad King Ludwig Palaces of Mad King Ludwig is a tile-laying, castle-building game for two to four players. This game is reminiscent of Carcassonne, except it is a good bit more complicated, requiring players to place building tiles near each other in specific patterns to earn swans of various colors, utilize special powers or scoring rules, and to build both above and below ground while the moat around the castle continually encloses your playspace.

Ultimately, while the components are nice quality, there are quite a lot of bits for a game like this, and the artwork is not particularly interesting. Rooms are largely void of identifiable decoration, making the words easy to read, but the rooms difficult to distinguish. Also of note, in the previous "Mad King" game, a major selling point of the game was mismatched and oddly sized tiles, while this one is entirely composed of squares and rectangles.

All told, we fell like this was a solid game, but one that has just a few too many rules that confine what you can do and what you want to do. Most of the time, there was a clear "best move" available, and rarely were more than, say, three decisions even possible based on what you could buy and where you could place it. I think a lot of people will like this game more than I did, as my fellow players certainly did. I would personally rather play something that is more streamlined (Carcassonne), or simply more interesting (Castles of Mad King Ludwig).

Also of note, Palace of Mad King Ludwig is not related to it's cousin "Castles," which is a little confusing. The idea behind the games is radically different.
text_fidelity_b: Bezier Games Palace of Mad King Ludwig

text_fidelity_a:
Crayola Mini Neon Marker Maker, 36 Scented Markers, Gift for Kids, Ages 6, 7, 8, 9 This is a great kit. It comes with enough marker-making equipment to make 36 markers, which will last you quite a while. We've played twice with this kit since getting it, and we still have equipment left for making more. The markers themselves are small, and they won't last all that long, but long enough for plenty of use. Everything is very good in terms of quality of components, and ease of making the markers.

One small gripe: making your own colors (i.e. combinations that are not on the helpful color-making sheet they include) is likely going to be a fail. We haven't made a lot of progress in terms of making brown (should be easy, right? - ours looks blue or green), black or even just blends and variations on purple and blue. They tend to look a mess. I guess that's why the color chart is included.

Overall, this is a great kit that will provide hours of entertainment, even for those "too old" to color. It teaches the basics of color mixing and color theory, and is easy for kids to do on their own with minimal supervision. We made a mess too, and it's easy to wipe up!
text_fidelity_b: Crayola Mini Neon Marker Maker, 36 Scented Markers, Gift for Kids, Ages 6, 7, 8, 9

text_fidelity_a:
Tokaido Board Game (Base Game) | Strategy Game | Travel Adventure Game | Exploration Game for Adults and Teens | Ages 8+ | 2-5 Players | Average Playtime 45 Minutes | Made by Funforge Simple, serene and elegant, this is a game like few others in your collection. This one is about a trip through Japan, and has very nice Japanese style artwork that really pops. One look at the box cover will tell you how elegant and evocative this game is, and that really is one of it's finest features.

Gameplay is rather simple. Those who rush ahead to see the sights first certainly get some kind of advantage - they often get first choice of where to go - while those who take their time will have plenty of opportunity to catch up, as the last player is always the next to move, meaning that travellers who venture too far out will allow others to make every stop along the way. There are "safe" and predictable options where you always get two or three points, and there are gambling options where you might be able to buy cards that give you far more.

It's a good, simple game that works well as a gateway game, but like many games, it says it's a decent two-player game, and I don't think that it is. It shines with three to four players. The decisions are not particularly deep or exciting, and much of the time, there really are only two choices that you can choose from - move really slow, or move really fast - and those choices are often easy to make.

If you're a gamer, I don't think you'll like this game. You can find better gateway games for sure, and there are thousands of games where you'll make more interesting choices. If you're just getting into games, or if you need something new to play with grandma, then this might be the best choice you can make.
text_fidelity_b: Tokaido Board Game (Base Game) | Strategy Game | Travel Adventure Game | Exploration Game for Adults and Teens | Ages 8+ | 2-5 Players | Average Playtime 45 Minutes | Made by Funforge

text_fidelity_a:
Civilization A New Dawn Board Game | Tactical Strategy Game for Adults and Teens Based on the Hit Video Game Series | Ages 14+ | 2-4 Players | Average Playtime 1-2 Hours | Made by Fantasy Flight Games Civilization: A New Dawn is indeed a new dawn in board gaming for this tried and true franchise. The Sid Meier property has had multiple iterations of previous games, each briging more and more complexity to the table. A New Dawn dials that back a good deal, abstracting many concepts, and doing away with large numbers of pieces and systems in favor of a more streamlined, simple and abstracted system.

And in almost every case, this new system works extremely well. Science and technology is particularly interesting to play with, requiring you to make great sacrfices in power and ability to move up the track in search of new ability. Even the game's winning conditions are easier to understand - the game's goal cards have two halves, and simply by fulfilling one side of each of three cards, you'll earn a victory. These neat and tidy new systems removed huge numbers of pieces from the game, and made the whole thing fit into a nice smaller sized box with a modular board for exploration, a nice touch from previous editions, many of which took place on a fairly boring board that looked like a small island.

The one area where the streamlining process fails, and where that failure comes down quite hard, is in the military systems. There is still a combat mechanic in the game, but because the game took away so many of the unit pieces and simplified down the fighting system, there is very little strategy, and many game-altering battles will be a simple "who rolls higher" contest with no modifiers or rerolls. This takes an otherwise strategic and highly contested game and breaks it all down to luck, ruining a large part of the experience for many.

This fatal flaw in the game is a big reason for my dislike of the game, but the game overall is quite good. It's a shame that this one element is going to make the game so polarizing. It's fun to a certain extent, but it does quite frequently just come down to randomness at the end.
text_fidelity_b: Civilization A New Dawn Board Game | Tactical Strategy Game for Adults and Teens Based on the Hit Video Game Series | Ages 14+ | 2-4 Players | Average Playtime 1-2 Hours | Made by Fantasy Flight Games

Learning Resources Botley The Coding Robot - 45 Pieces, Ages 5+ Screen- Free Coding Toys, Coding STEM Toy for Kids, Coding for Kids,Back to School Gifts,Teacher Supplies Botley is quite a versatile fellow.

My four year old is having fun running him around in "line" mode, where his sensors follow a black lined path on a white background. When he reaches the end, he turns around and comes back.

Daddy is having a little more fun with "code" mode, which is too complex for the little one at this point. You program multiple commands into the remote, and then you send Botley out on a small adventure, around the obstacle course pieces that you can set up with material from the box. It's simple and easy for an adult, but for kids, it will teach computer programming basics, planning ahead, and thinking before you act.

text_fidelity_a:
CGE Czech Games Edition Thats A Question Excellent party game from the makers of Codenames. If you've played Codenames, then you know that is a fantastic party game, but that it requires the right group - a slow or domineering player can often mean that everyone is standing around staring at the board for an hour while they dole out perfectly configured clues. It's a fun game, but it requires the right group. That's a Question is a party game that can be played by absolutely anyone, and that, in my opinion, makes it almost a superior game.

In That's a Question!, players use cards to ask A/B style "would you rather" questions in which players attempt to guess the outcome. Based on the results, you move your pawn along the track.

The rulebook is well-written and funny, and is aware that this game is a little bit weird - attempting to give a theme to a basic Q&A style game, but it works. Of course, the game is not perfect. You are limited to only asking three different main questions, although the game does provide a wide variation of answers. There are also point modification questions which allow you to muddy up the scoring in your favor. Ultimately, the scoring was the part of the game that we found most cumbersome, and the modifiers didn't help that, simply adding a little more chaos. Scoring is also modified based on how many players are playing; as this was clearly designed as a 5-6 player game, a 4-player game has a few modifications, and the 3-player game has a fairly substantial number of scoring modifications to make it more challenging. It's nothing you can't figure out, but it is not very clean.

Overall, a good party game for 5-6. The box indicates that this is a game for ages 15+, and nothing in the content of the cards makes me think that anyone from age 7 and up can't handle.
text_fidelity_b: CGE Czech Games Edition Thats A Question

text_fidelity_a:
Educational Insights Kanoodle Jr. Brain Boosting Puzzle Game, Brain Teaser Game for Kids Teens, & Adults, 2-D & 3-D Puzzles, Great For Travel, Gift For Kids Ages 4 to 7 What a great puzzle. Kanoodle is a one-player game in which you take 6 tetris-like pieces and use them to fill in a pattern on the square board. There are 60 puzzles in this group, all included in a book form. I do have a few minor issues, enough to remove one star:

- The puzzles are delivered in the form of a book. There are multiple languages of instructions inside, then you get to the puzzles. Each puzzle is well-done, but the book itself is not the ideal way of presenting the puzzles. Since you're either balancing the book on the shelf above the board, or pulling it out or putting it back underneath the board, it gets scuffed, torn and bent up rather quickly. On day 3, our book looks like a mess. It should have been thicker cards with a separate rulebook.

- Some kids will master this quickly. My four-year-old is on 4-star puzzles already, and we've owned the game for less than 3 days. I think she'll be stuck here for a decent while, and she does enjoy going back to re-do easier puzzles, but I think she's got the hang of it quickly. Yesterday, she completed puzzle 43 out of 60, and they're ordered by difficulty.

This review may sound negative, but let me emphasize that THIS IS SUCH A GOOD TOY! You can see the wheels turning in my daughter's brain as she tries to figure out how to make it work. If you're going on a road trip, this is a must.
text_fidelity_b: Educational Insights Kanoodle Jr. Brain Boosting Puzzle Game, Brain Teaser Game for Kids Teens, & Adults, 2-D & 3-D Puzzles, Great For Travel, Gift For Kids Ages 4 to 7

text_fidelity_a:
Sherlock Holmes Consulting Detective: Jack the Ripper & West End Adventures Standalone Game The predecessor to this game, Sherlock Holmes: Consulting Detective, is my all-time favorite game, and holds a high place on my game shelf despite being a “one and done” experience. Does this new iteration hold up to the high standard the previous game established?

To start with, the production value on this new version is heads and shoulders above the 2013 edition of SHCD that I own. The paper is printed on much nicer stock, the box is thicker and better designed to hold the contents, and the instruction manual in particular shows a great attention to detail that the previous edition lacked. I particularly like that in this edition, the solutions to each case are printed upside down in the back of the box, and that the solutions are encased in an envelope secured to each case book to prevent spoiling any aspects of the story with erroneous page turns.

Like the previous game, this “board game” is much more of a “choose your own adventure” story for you and your friends to solve. Each case is represented by a book, in which you’re given an introductory story, and then allowed free reign to investigate a variety of leads and allies to assist you in gathering information about whodunit. Once you think you know what’s happening, turn to the questions and find out what happened in this story – don’t worry, there are significant explanations and story to give closure to each case.

This is a stand-alone game, meaning that if you haven’t already played the original SHCD, you can purchase this with no strings attached. I don’t think I would recommend that for new players, however.

Jack the Ripper and the West End Adventures are quite different from what you get in the original game. In the original, there were some threads of story that remained from one case to the next, but in the new version, four of the cases are designed to be played campaign-style in an effort to solve the Jack the Ripper murders.

I’m sure that there will be many people out there who love the Jack the Ripper campaign - a set of four cases that are thematically tied together that will allow you to hunt down Jack using a separate map and additional investigative helpers – but it really isn’t for me. First of all, the cases are quite a bit darker and less whimsical than your traditional Sherlock Holmes story and case, and are tied together only by the fact that they occur in the same area and time period. I think the original cases are too difficult to be played by, let’s say, a 10 year old, but the stories wouldn’t be inappropriate for them in terms of language and description. The Jack cases, on the other hand, would carry a definite R-rating – they’re well-researched historically, and include lots of graphic description and a few cuss words as well. If you know anything about the historical Jack cases, you’d probably know this going in, but if you’re used to the style of the original cases, know that this is a darker affair. Secondly, you absolutely cannot find Jack and get a satisfactory conclusion until the fourth case, which is a decent investment in time with little return for parts 1 - 3. Third, and this is the big reason I didn’t like it, is that the mini-mysteries you’re solving in parts 1, 2 and 3 are not mysteries at all, but historical backstory. The questions are answered directly by particular sources, so if you visit the right allies and pursue the right leads you will simply be given the correct answers to each piece without putting much of anything together outside of remembering what the leads gave you. This was a very different experience, with a different writing style, different thematic elements, and a wholly different style, and since I am such a fan of the tried-and-true SHCD formula, I did not enjoy it as much as others may.

The other six cases are all stand-alone cases, and are quite good, although in most cases, they’re quite a bit harder than the already difficult cases in the original box. Like that set, some are better than others, but I will admit that the overall quality of these cases is on-par with what came in the original box, but still harder. I don’t think this is the right place to start with the SHCD universe.

Therein lies the only real problem that I have with this SHCD set – that while packaged as a stand-alone, this game is put together in a way that strongly suggests that it’s a sequel. If you think of it in movie terms, sure, you can watch most sequels without seeing the original movies, but why would you, especially if you know going in that watching the original is going to improve your experience? The cases in this box are more difficult, and the Jack the Ripper set is an odd starting place.

Overall, this game comes very highly recommended to any fan of the original set of cases. If this game sounds like something you’d be interested in, get it, but be advised that I think that the original set of 10 cases are a superior starting place.

4.5/5
text_fidelity_b: Sherlock Holmes Consulting Detective: Jack the Ripper & West End Adventures Standalone Game
